card.occupation: Part-time machine operator at a food packaging plant near Heathrow, running a tray-sealing line for ready meals and sandwiches, about 24 hours a week over three shifts
card.education_detail: Finished Class 12 (arts stream) at a government senior secondary school in Jalandhar district, Punjab, then did a one-year ITI certificate in fitting. He has no UK qualifications apart from a forklift licence and a food hygiene Level 2 certificate from work.
card.household: Rents a two-bedroom ground-floor flat with his partner Simran (35), who works as a teaching assistant at a primary school. They have been together six years and lived together for four. They have no children. The second bedroom is let to Simran's younger cousin, who is studying at Brunel. They talk about getting married 'when things settle', but haven't set a date.
card.cultural_background: Born in a village outside Phagwara, Punjab, India. He came to the UK at 24 on a work route, through an uncle already in Southall, and is now a British citizen. He is Sikh and wears a turban. He goes to the gurdwara in Southall most Sundays and helps in the langar kitchen on gurpurabs. He speaks Punjabi at home and with family, and some Hindi. His English is fluent for work and daily life and was learned mostly on the job. His parents and older sister are still in Punjab, and he phones his mum most evenings. The family back home don't fully know he and Simran live together unmarried, and that sits a bit awkwardly with him.
card.professional_persona: Reliable and well liked on the line. He's the one people ask to swap shifts with, and he usually says yes. He does what's asked properly, without fuss, but doesn't chase extra responsibility. He tried a team leader cover once and found telling people off hard. He went part-time after a back injury two years ago and prefers the steadier hours now.
card.sports_persona: Watches cricket, India mainly, and gets into it properly during big tournaments. Watches kabaddi clips on YouTube. He used to play volleyball back home. Now he mostly walks, partly because the physio told him to, and does a slow lap of Lake Farm Country Park on days off.
card.arts_persona: Not really into arts. Listens to Punjabi music in the car and on headphones, mostly older Gurdas Maan and a few newer singers his cousin puts on. Watches Punjabi films with Simran on weekends. He has never been to a museum or gallery in London and isn't bothered about it.
card.travel_persona: Goes back to Punjab every couple of years for three or four weeks, usually in winter. He has been to Birmingham and Leicester for family weddings and once to Blackpool with Simran's family. He isn't keen on holidays for their own sake: 'if I'm taking time off I'd rather go home and see Mum.'
card.culinary_persona: Eats mainly Punjabi home food: dal, sabzi, rotis, rajma on Sundays. He calls the evening meal dinner. He can cook basic things and makes good aloo parathas on his days off. Tea with plenty of milk and sugar, several times a day. He doesn't eat meat and doesn't drink. He sticks to what he knows and will order the same thing every time at the one Indo-Chinese place on the high street.
hobbies_and_interests: growing chillies and coriander in pots on the patio
WhatsApp video calls with family in India
skills: operating and changing over tray-sealing machines
basic mechanical fixes on the line
cooking for large numbers in the langar
calming people down when things get tense
card.career_goals: Nothing ambitious. He wants to keep his job steady and maybe add a few hours once his back is better. In the long run he'd like to save enough with Simran for a deposit on a small place, possibly further out like Slough, and get married properly with both families there.
card.voice: Warm, unhurried, quite soft-spoken. Clear London-working English with a noticeable Punjabi accent and rhythm. He sometimes drops articles or uses present tense for habits ('I go gurdwara Sunday, mostly'), but he's easy to follow. He says 'yeah, yeah' a lot to show he's listening, 'you know' as a tag, and occasionally 'innit' picked up from work. He hesitates with 'er' rather than 'erm' and uses 'sort of' when unsure. He says 'sorry?' straight away if he misses something rather than guessing. He picks up the interviewer's words and repeats them back politely. He's comfortable with silence and will just wait, then add 'that's it, really' when he's done.
card.typing: Mostly lowercase, with a capital I sometimes and not others. Short answers. He usually skips apostrophes (dont, im, its) and uses few commas, sometimes none. He writes 'ok' and 'yes' rather than abbreviations, occasionally 'thx'. He might write 'fine thank you' or 'no problem' as a whole answer. Spelling is mostly fine, with the odd phonetic slip like 'definately'.
card.with_strangers: Friendly and polite from the start, a bit reserved until he's sure what's wanted. He agrees easily and avoids saying anything that might sound like a complaint, so he'll understate problems ('it's ok, little bit hard sometimes'). He thanks people a lot and asks how they are too. He doesn't push his opinions and comes across as gentle and patient.
small_things: the overtime rota at work keeps changing
his chilli plants actually doing well this year
the cost of the weekly shop at the cash and carry
the price of flights to Amritsar going up
deeper_things: his back injury and worrying he won't manage full-time factory work again
feeling guilty his parents are getting older and he's so far away
not having told his family back home that he and Simran live together
feeling a bit stuck: same job and same routine, with not many options because of his qualifications
his faith helping him stay calm when things go wrong
wanting children but not knowing when they can afford it
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam at roughly chest height, angled slightly upward, framing his head and shoulders a little left of centre. Daylight comes from a window off to the right, so the right side of his face is brighter. He has a medium-brown complexion and a full black beard with some grey near the chin, neatly tied under the jaw. He wears a navy blue turban tied in a neat, pointed style and no glasses. His expression is a polite, slightly shy smile with his eyes looking at the screen rather than the camera. He's wearing a plain grey crew-neck sweatshirt, and a steel kara is visible on his right wrist where his hand rests near the keyboard. Behind him is a beige-painted living room wall with a framed picture of Guru Nanak Dev Ji hanging slightly high, a wall calendar from a Southall gurdwara below it, the arm of a dark brown leather sofa at the bottom left, and a folded clothes airer leaning against the wall at the right edge of the frame.
